notes.h: Perioperative care: assessment, optimisation and postoperative complications
notes.body:
Perioperative care runs from the decision to operate to full recovery.

Preoperative assessment:
- History and examination focused on cardiorespiratory reserve (exercise tolerance, for example climbing two flights of stairs), airway, previous anaesthetics and family history of anaesthetic problems.
- ASA physical status: I healthy; II mild systemic disease; III severe systemic disease; IV severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life; V moribund, not expected to survive without the operation; VI brain-dead organ donor. Add "E" for emergency surgery.
- Investigations guided by NICE NG45 (2016) according to the grade of surgery and comorbidity, rather than routine tests for everyone. Always do a pregnancy test where relevant, and group and save or crossmatch according to expected blood loss.
- Fasting: usually 6 hours for food and 2 hours for clear fluids in adults.

Medication management:
- Anticoagulants and antiplatelets: weigh bleeding against thrombotic risk; bridging is reserved for high thrombotic risk.
- Diabetes: follow the Centre for Perioperative Care (CPOC) guidance. SGLT2 inhibitors are omitted the day before and the day of surgery because of the risk of euglycaemic ketoacidosis. Use a variable-rate insulin infusion if more than one meal will be missed or control is poor.
- Long-term steroids: give perioperative steroid cover to avoid adrenal crisis.

VTE prevention (NICE NG89): assess every patient's VTE and bleeding risk on admission. Options are mechanical (anti-embolism stockings, intermittent pneumatic compression) and pharmacological (low molecular weight heparin, DOACs after joint replacement). Extended prophylaxis is used after hip and knee replacement and major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery.

Safety and recovery: the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist has three pauses: sign in (before induction), time out (before incision) and sign out (before leaving theatre). Enhanced recovery (ERAS) bundles include preoperative carbohydrate loading, minimal fasting, opioid-sparing analgesia, goal-directed fluids, early feeding and early mobilisation.

Postoperative complications by timing:
- Immediate (within 24 hours): primary haemorrhage, anaesthetic complications, basal atelectasis.
- Early (days 1–7): fever from atelectasis or the inflammatory response in the first 48 hours; pneumonia, urinary infection and line infection from about day 3; surgical site infection and anastomotic leak around days 5–7; ileus; AKI; delirium.
- Any time from a few days onwards: DVT and PE.
- Late: incisional hernia, adhesions.

Worked example: on day 6 after an anterior resection, a patient becomes tachycardic, febrile and newly confused, with increasing abdominal pain. The timing and signs point to an anastomotic leak until proven otherwise: start sepsis care and arrange urgent CT and surgical review.

Pitfalls: attributing tachycardia to pain without excluding bleeding, leak or PE; forgetting to restart withheld medications; missing urinary retention as a cause of confusion.

notes.h: The acute abdomen: assessment, appendicitis, pancreatitis, biliary disease and obstruction
notes.body:
Approach: resuscitate first, then localise. Generalised peritonitis (rigid abdomen, guarding, patient lying still) suggests perforation. Colicky pain with restlessness suggests a hollow-organ cause such as renal or biliary colic or obstruction.

Core investigations: FBC, U&E, CRP, LFTs, amylase or lipase, lactate, group and save, urinalysis, and a pregnancy test in every woman of childbearing age. Imaging: erect chest X-ray for free gas; CT abdomen and pelvis is the workhorse in adults; ultrasound for biliary disease and in children and pregnant women.

Appendicitis: periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, low-grade fever, tenderness at McBurney's point, and positive Rovsing's or psoas signs. Scores such as Alvarado support assessment. Ultrasound is useful in children and young women. Laparoscopic appendicectomy is standard. The CODA trial (2020) showed that antibiotics are a reasonable alternative for selected uncomplicated cases, although some patients later need surgery, especially if an appendicolith is present.

Acute pancreatitis: diagnosis needs two of three (revised Atlanta classification, 2012): characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back; amylase or lipase at least 3 times the upper limit of normal; and characteristic imaging. Commonest causes are gallstones and alcohol. Severity is assessed with the Glasgow–Imrie score (PANCREAS: PaO₂ <8 kPa, age >55, neutrophils/WCC >15, calcium <2 mmol/L, renal urea >16 mmol/L, enzymes LDH >600 or AST >200, albumin <32 g/L, sugar >10 mmol/L); 3 or more within 48 hours predicts severe disease. Management is supportive: fluids, analgesia, monitoring, early enteral nutrition, and no routine prophylactic antibiotics. Urgent ERCP is used for coexisting cholangitis. Cholecystectomy follows during the same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis.

Biliary disease:
- Biliary colic: RUQ pain after fatty meals, lasting hours, without systemic upset.
- Acute cholecystitis: persistent RUQ pain, fever and Murphy's sign. NICE CG188 recommends laparoscopic cholecystectomy within a week of diagnosis.
- Ascending cholangitis: Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain); Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension and confusion. Treat with antibiotics and biliary drainage, usually ERCP.

Bowel obstruction: colicky pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation. Small-bowel causes are mainly adhesions and hernias; large-bowel causes are cancer and volvulus. The "3-6-9" rule gives upper normal diameters of small bowel, colon and caecum in cm. Initial care is IV fluids, NG decompression and analgesia ("drip and suck"); CT confirms the site and cause. Strangulation, closed-loop obstruction or peritonism needs surgery. Sigmoid volvulus (coffee-bean sign) is usually decompressed endoscopically first.

Worked example: a 68-year-old in AF with severe abdominal pain, a soft abdomen and lactate 6 mmol/L may have acute mesenteric ischaemia. Pain out of proportion to signs is the clue, and CT angiography is needed.

Pitfalls: forgetting the pregnancy test (ectopic pregnancy); missing a ruptured AAA in an older patient with "renal colic"; relying on amylase late in pancreatitis.

notes.h: Gastrointestinal surgery: colorectal and upper GI cancer, hernias and anorectal disease
notes.body:
Colorectal cancer is the fourth commonest cancer in the UK. Risk factors include age, family history, inherited syndromes (Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis), inflammatory bowel disease, red and processed meat, obesity, smoking and alcohol. Right-sided tumours often present with iron-deficiency anaemia; left-sided and rectal tumours present with change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding or obstruction.

Detection:
- Symptomatic patients in primary care: quantitative faecal immunochemical testing (FIT). A result of 10 µg Hb/g faeces or above prompts referral on the suspected cancer pathway (NICE DG56, 2023).
- Screening: the NHS Bowel Cancer Screening Programme sends home FIT kits every two years to people aged 50–74 in England, after the age extension from 60. The screening referral threshold is much higher than the symptomatic one: England has used 120 µg Hb/g and is lowering it to 80 µg Hb/g in a phased rollout due to finish by March 2028 (Scotland and Wales already use 80).
- Staging: colonoscopy with biopsy, CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, and pelvic MRI for rectal cancer. Staging uses TNM.

Operations by tumour site:
- Caecum, ascending colon or hepatic flexure: right hemicolectomy.
- Transverse colon: extended right hemicolectomy.
- Descending colon: left hemicolectomy.
- Sigmoid or upper rectum: high anterior resection.
- Mid and lower rectum: low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision, often with a defunctioning loop ileostomy.
- Tumours invading the anal sphincters: abdominoperineal resection with a permanent end colostomy.
- Emergency (perforation, obstruction) left-sided disease: Hartmann's procedure (resection, end colostomy, rectal stump closed).

Stomas: ileostomies are spouted (small-bowel contents are irritant) and usually sit in the right iliac fossa; colostomies are flush and usually sit in the left iliac fossa.

Upper GI cancer: oesophageal adenocarcinoma (lower third; linked to reflux, Barrett's oesophagus and obesity) is now commoner in the UK than squamous cell carcinoma (upper and middle thirds; smoking and alcohol).

Hernias:
- Indirect inguinal: passes through the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, may enter the scrotum, and is the commonest type in both sexes.
- Direct inguinal: pushes through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
- Inguinal hernias emerge above and medial to the pubic tubercle; femoral hernias emerge below and lateral to it. Femoral hernias are commoner in women, have a narrow neck, carry a high strangulation risk, and are repaired promptly.

Anorectal conditions: haemorrhoids (painless bright red bleeding); anal fissure (pain on defecation, usually posterior midline; topical GTN or diltiazem, then botulinum toxin or sphincterotomy); perianal abscess (incision and drainage); fistula-in-ano (Goodsall's rule predicts the internal opening); pilonidal sinus.

Worked example: an 80-year-old with iron-deficiency anaemia, no bowel symptoms and FIT 85 µg Hb/g needs urgent referral; a caecal tumour would be treated with right hemicolectomy.

Pitfalls: confusing direct and indirect hernias with femoral; describing a spouted stoma in the left iliac fossa as a colostomy without checking the output; ignoring anaemia as a presentation of right-sided cancer.

notes.h: Vascular surgery: peripheral arterial disease, acute limb ischaemia, AAA, carotid and venous disease
notes.body:
Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) is atherosclerosis of the limb arteries. Intermittent claudication is reproducible muscle pain on walking, relieved by rest. Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) means rest pain (often at night, eased by hanging the leg down), ulceration or gangrene.

Ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI) = highest ankle systolic pressure ÷ highest brachial systolic pressure:
- Below 0.9 indicates PAD; below about 0.5 indicates severe disease.
- Above about 1.3–1.4 suggests incompressible calcified vessels (diabetes, CKD), which falsely reassure; use toe pressures instead.

PAD management (NICE CG147): stop smoking, a statin, an antiplatelet (clopidogrel is usually preferred), and control of blood pressure and diabetes. Offer a supervised exercise programme for claudication. Angioplasty with or without stenting, or bypass surgery, is used for lifestyle-limiting symptoms despite this and for CLTI.

Acute limb ischaemia presents with the "6 Ps": pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishing cold, paraesthesia and paralysis. Embolism (often from AF) causes sudden onset with no history of claudication. Thrombosis in situ occurs in an already diseased artery, with prior claudication and collaterals. Give IV unfractionated heparin and get urgent vascular review. Treatment is embolectomy, catheter-directed thrombolysis or bypass. Sensory loss and paralysis indicate a threatened limb needing emergency revascularisation; fixed mottling suggests irreversible ischaemia. After reperfusion, watch for compartment syndrome (fasciotomy) and hyperkalaemia.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA): aortic diameter of 3.0 cm or more. The NHS AAA Screening Programme offers men a single ultrasound in the year they turn 65.
- 3.0–4.4 cm: yearly ultrasound.
- 4.5–5.4 cm: three-monthly ultrasound.
- 5.5 cm or more, growth over 1 cm a year, or symptoms: refer to the vascular service, to be seen within 2 weeks.
Repair is open or endovascular (EVAR); NICE NG156 (2020) weighs anatomy, fitness and lifelong surveillance needs. Rupture presents with abdominal or back pain, collapse and a pulsatile mass. It needs permissive hypotension, a major haemorrhage protocol and immediate transfer for repair.

Carotid disease: after a TIA or non-disabling stroke, patients with symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50–99% (NASCET criteria) should be assessed and referred urgently for carotid endarterectomy, with surgery ideally within 2 weeks of symptom onset (NICE NG128).

Venous disease: varicose veins causing symptoms or skin changes are referred for duplex scanning; endothermal ablation is first-line (NICE CG168). Venous leg ulcers, in the gaiter area, are treated with compression after arterial disease has been excluded with an ABPI.

Worked example: ankle pressures 70 and 64 mmHg, brachial pressures 140 and 132 mmHg. ABPI = 70 ÷ 140 = 0.5, at the threshold for severe PAD. Full compression is generally only used when the ABPI is about 0.8 or above, so compression bandaging would be unsafe.

Pitfalls: being reassured by a high ABPI in a diabetic patient; applying compression without an ABPI; labelling a ruptured AAA as renal colic.

notes.h: Urology: stones, the acute scrotum, prostate disease and urological cancer
notes.body:
Renal colic: sudden severe loin-to-groin pain with restlessness, often with haematuria. NICE NG118 (2019) recommends NSAIDs as first-line analgesia (by any route), low-dose non-contrast CT KUB within 24 hours of presentation, and ultrasound in pregnancy and children. Alpha-blockers can help distal ureteric stones under 10 mm pass. Intervention options are shockwave lithotripsy, ureteroscopy, and percutaneous nephrolithotomy for large renal stones (over 2 cm).

An obstructed, infected kidney (fever or sepsis with a ureteric stone) is a urological emergency. It needs antibiotics and urgent decompression by nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent.

Acute scrotum:
- Testicular torsion: commonest in adolescents. Sudden severe testicular pain, often with vomiting; the testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie and the cremasteric reflex is absent. It is a clinical diagnosis: go straight to surgical exploration, ideally within 6 hours, with bilateral fixation. Do not delay for ultrasound.
- Epididymo-orchitis: more gradual onset with urinary or STI symptoms. Causes are chlamydia and gonorrhoea in younger men and enteric organisms in older men.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia: lower urinary tract symptoms. Voiding symptoms are hesitancy, poor stream and terminal dribbling; storage symptoms are frequency, urgency and nocturia. Alpha-blockers relax prostatic smooth muscle and work within days. 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors shrink an enlarged prostate over months and roughly halve PSA. TURP or other procedures are used for refractory symptoms, retention or complications.

Acute urinary retention: painful inability to void with a palpable bladder. Catheterise and record the residual volume; start an alpha-blocker before a trial without catheter.

Prostate cancer: usually adenocarcinoma of the peripheral zone. Investigate a raised age-adjusted PSA or abnormal DRE with multiparametric MRI before biopsy (NICE NG131). Grade with the Gleason/ISUP grade group and risk-stratify with the Cambridge Prognostic Groups. Options include active surveillance, radical prostatectomy and radiotherapy, with androgen deprivation therapy for higher-risk or metastatic disease.

Other urological cancers:
- Bladder: painless visible haematuria; risk factors are smoking and occupational aromatic amines. Investigate with flexible cystoscopy and CT urography. Adults aged 45 or over with unexplained visible haematuria (no UTI) go on the suspected cancer pathway (NICE NG12).
- Renal cell carcinoma: often found incidentally; classic triad of haematuria, loin pain and mass.
- Testicular germ cell tumours (seminoma, non-seminomatous): painless lump in young men. Markers are AFP, β-hCG and LDH; AFP is not raised in pure seminoma. Treated by radical inguinal orchidectomy, never scrotal biopsy.

Worked example: a 15-year-old with 3 hours of left testicular pain and vomiting has a high-riding testis and absent cremasteric reflex. He needs scrotal exploration now; ultrasound would only waste salvage time.

Pitfalls: forgetting that 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors lower PSA; managing an infected obstructed kidney with analgesia alone; ordering imaging for suspected torsion.

notes.h: Breast surgery: assessment, benign disease and breast cancer
notes.body:
Triple assessment is the standard for any breast symptom:
- Clinical: history and examination of both breasts and axillae.
- Imaging: mammography, usually with ultrasound, in women aged 40 and over; ultrasound alone is usually first-line in younger women, whose denser breasts make mammography less sensitive.
- Pathology: core needle biopsy (or fine-needle aspiration for cysts or nodes).

NICE NG12 referral: people aged 30 and over with an unexplained breast lump, or aged 50 and over with discharge, retraction or other concerning change in one nipple only, should be referred on the suspected cancer pathway.

Screening: the NHS Breast Screening Programme invites women from 50 to their 71st birthday for mammography every three years.

Benign conditions:
- Fibroadenoma: smooth, mobile, rubbery lump in young women; confirm with imaging and biopsy, and excise only if large, growing or symptomatic.
- Cysts: commonest in women aged 40–50; aspirate if symptomatic and investigate further if the fluid is bloodstained or a lump remains.
- Lactational mastitis or abscess: usually Staphylococcus aureus. Continue breastfeeding; treat an abscess with ultrasound-guided aspiration and antibiotics.
- Periductal mastitis (smokers), duct ectasia (older women), intraductal papilloma (single-duct bloody discharge) and fat necrosis (after trauma, may mimic cancer).

Breast cancer: commonest cancer in UK women. Risk factors include age, family history, BRCA1/2 mutations, early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, HRT, obesity and alcohol. Invasive ductal carcinoma of no special type is the commonest type. Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is non-invasive and often found as microcalcification on screening.

Receptor status guides therapy: oestrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor and HER2. Triple-negative cancers are commoner with BRCA1 mutations and have no targeted endocrine or HER2 option.

Management (NICE NG101):
- Surgery: breast-conserving surgery (wide local excision) plus radiotherapy gives survival equivalent to mastectomy for suitable tumours. The axilla is staged with sentinel lymph node biopsy if clinically and ultrasound node-negative; proven nodal disease usually needs axillary treatment (clearance or radiotherapy).
- Endocrine therapy for ER-positive disease: tamoxifen (a selective oestrogen receptor modulator; raises VTE and endometrial cancer risk) or aromatase inhibitors in postmenopausal women (bone loss and arthralgia; monitor bone density).
- HER2-positive disease: trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody against HER2; monitor cardiac function because of cardiotoxicity.
- Chemotherapy, neoadjuvant or adjuvant, according to risk.

Nottingham Prognostic Index = (0.2 × tumour size in cm) + grade (1–3) + nodal score (1 = no nodes, 2 = 1–3 nodes, 3 = 4 or more). Example: a 2.5 cm grade 2 tumour with two involved nodes gives 0.5 + 2 + 2 = 4.5. Lower scores mean a better prognosis.

Pitfalls: performing mammography first in a 25-year-old; assuming a benign-feeling lump needs no biopsy; forgetting bone protection with aromatase inhibitors.

notes.h: Orthopaedics and trauma: trauma care, hip fractures, open fractures and emergencies
notes.body:
Major trauma follows ATLS principles: a primary survey of <C>ABCDE (catastrophic haemorrhage first), with treatment as problems are found, followed by a secondary survey.

Describing a fracture: patient and X-ray details, bone and side, location (diaphyseal, metaphyseal, intra-articular), pattern (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted), displacement, angulation, rotation and shortening, and whether it is open or closed. Always assess neurovascular status.

Open fractures (BOAST 2017): IV antibiotics as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour of injury; photograph the wound, apply a saline-soaked dressing, splint the limb and check tetanus status. Debride immediately for highly contaminated wounds or vascular injury, within 12 hours for high-energy injuries and within 24 hours for others.

Hip fractures (NICE CG124): usually older people falling from standing height.
- Intracapsular fractures (Garden I–II undisplaced, III–IV displaced) can disrupt the retinacular blood supply from the medial circumflex femoral artery, causing avascular necrosis. Displaced fractures are treated with arthroplasty: total hip replacement for people who walked independently outdoors with no more than a stick, are not cognitively impaired and are medically fit; otherwise hemiarthroplasty. Undisplaced fractures may be fixed with screws.
- Extracapsular trochanteric fractures: sliding hip screw; subtrochanteric fractures: intramedullary nail.
- Operate on the day of or the day after admission, with orthogeriatric care, early mobilisation and a falls and bone-health assessment.

Other key injuries:
- Scaphoid fracture: anatomical snuffbox tenderness after a fall on an outstretched hand. Initial X-rays may be normal; immobilise and arrange MRI. The retrograde blood supply puts the proximal pole at risk of avascular necrosis.
- Anterior shoulder dislocation: check axillary nerve sensation over the "regimental badge" area before and after reduction.
- Supracondylar humeral fracture in children: risk to the brachial artery and median/anterior interosseous nerve.
- Ottawa ankle rules: X-ray if there is malleolar pain plus bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to bear weight both immediately and in the department.

Orthopaedic emergencies:
- Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch; pulses are often present. Split the cast to skin and arrange urgent fasciotomy.
- Cauda equina syndrome: bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction; emergency MRI and decompression.
- Septic arthritis: hot, swollen, painful joint. Aspirate before antibiotics; Staphylococcus aureus is commonest. Joint washout is needed.

Worked example: an 84-year-old who uses a stick outdoors and has mild dementia has a displaced intracapsular fracture. Cognitive impairment excludes total hip replacement, so cemented hemiarthroplasty is appropriate.

Pitfalls: being reassured by palpable pulses in compartment syndrome; discharging a suspected scaphoid fracture with a normal X-ray; delaying antibiotics in open fractures.

notes.h: Anaesthesia: airway, general and regional anaesthesia, and complications
notes.body:
General anaesthesia rests on the triad of hypnosis (unconsciousness), analgesia and muscle relaxation.

Airway assessment: Mallampati class, mouth opening, thyromental distance, neck movement, jaw protrusion, and a history of previous difficult intubation. NAP4 (2011) highlighted airway disasters and the rule "no trace = wrong place": waveform capnography must confirm every tracheal tube. Difficult Airway Society guidelines set out plans A–D, ending in front-of-neck access (scalpel cricothyroidotomy) in a "can't intubate, can't oxygenate" situation.

Induction agents:
- Propofol: potentiates GABA-A; smooth induction, antiemetic, but causes hypotension and pain on injection.
- Ketamine: NMDA antagonist; preserves blood pressure and airway reflexes, bronchodilates, provides analgesia; can cause emergence phenomena.

Maintenance: volatile agents (sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane) or total intravenous anaesthesia with propofol. Potency is expressed as minimum alveolar concentration (MAC), the concentration that prevents movement in response to surgical incision in 50% of patients. Nitrous oxide expands air-filled spaces, so it is avoided with pneumothorax or bowel obstruction.

Neuromuscular blockade:
- Suxamethonium is depolarising: rapid onset and short action. It causes fasciculations, hyperkalaemia (avoid in burns after the first day, crush injury and neuromuscular disease) and prolonged paralysis in pseudocholinesterase deficiency.
- Non-depolarising agents (rocuronium, atracurium; atracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination) compete at the nicotinic receptor. Reversal is with neostigmine (an anticholinesterase) given with glycopyrronium to block muscarinic effects, or with sugammadex, which encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium.

Rapid sequence induction is used when aspiration risk is high (emergency surgery, bowel obstruction, pregnancy, recent food): preoxygenation, an induction agent and a fast-acting neuromuscular blocker given together, with or without cricoid pressure, then intubation with a cuffed tube.

Malignant hyperthermia: autosomal dominant (often RYR1 mutations), triggered by volatile agents and suxamethonium. Signs are rising end-tidal CO₂, tachycardia, rigidity, hyperthermia and hyperkalaemia. Stop triggers and give dantrolene.

Regional and local anaesthesia: local anaesthetics block voltage-gated sodium channels. Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity causes perioral tingling, tinnitus, seizures and arrhythmias; stop injecting, support ABC and give lipid emulsion. Spinal anaesthesia injects into the subarachnoid space; epidural anaesthesia uses a catheter in the epidural space. Complications include hypotension from sympathetic block, post-dural puncture headache, high block, and rarely epidural haematoma or abscess. Coagulopathy, local infection and patient refusal are contraindications.

Postoperative nausea and vomiting: the Apfel score counts female sex, non-smoking, previous PONV or motion sickness, and postoperative opioids. Prophylaxis combines classes such as 5-HT₃ antagonists (ondansetron), dexamethasone and antihistamines (cyclizine).

Worked example: a patient with small-bowel obstruction needs a laparotomy. RSI is indicated, NG aspiration beforehand reduces gastric volume, and nitrous oxide should be avoided.

Pitfalls: giving suxamethonium to a patient with hyperkalaemia or a recent spinal cord injury; mistaking a spinal for an epidural; trusting chest movement rather than capnography.

cards.f: Describe ASA grades I–VI.
cards.b: I healthy; II mild systemic disease; III severe systemic disease; IV severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life; V moribund, not expected to survive without surgery; VI brain-dead organ donor. 'E' denotes emergency.

cards.f: What are standard adult preoperative fasting times?
cards.b: Usually 6 hours for food and 2 hours for clear fluids before elective anaesthesia.

cards.f: What are the three phases of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist?
cards.b: Sign in (before induction), time out (before skin incision) and sign out (before the patient leaves theatre).

cards.f: Why are SGLT2 inhibitors withheld around surgery?
cards.b: They can cause euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis during fasting and surgical stress; CPOC guidance omits them the day before and the day of surgery.

cards.f: Why do patients on long-term steroids need perioperative steroid cover?
cards.b: Exogenous steroids suppress the HPA axis, so they cannot mount a cortisol stress response and risk adrenal crisis with hypotension.

cards.f: What are the mechanical and pharmacological options for VTE prophylaxis?
cards.b: Mechanical: anti-embolism stockings and intermittent pneumatic compression. Pharmacological: low molecular weight heparin, or DOACs after joint replacement, according to NICE NG89 risk assessment.

cards.f: Give typical causes of postoperative fever by timing.
cards.b: First 48 hours: inflammatory response and atelectasis. From about day 3: pneumonia, UTI, line infection. Days 5–7: wound infection and anastomotic leak. VTE can occur at any time from a few days onwards.

cards.f: When does anastomotic leak classically present?
cards.b: Around days 5–7 after surgery, with tachycardia, fever, abdominal pain, ileus or confusion; investigate with CT and urgent surgical review.

cards.f: List four elements of an ERAS pathway.
cards.b: Preoperative carbohydrate loading and minimal fasting, opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, goal-directed fluid therapy, and early feeding and mobilisation.

cards.f: What does NICE NG45 say about preoperative tests?
cards.b: Tests should be selected by surgical grade and the patient's ASA status and comorbidity, not ordered routinely for everyone.

cards.f: Which test must every woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain have?
cards.b: A pregnancy test, to exclude ectopic pregnancy and inform imaging and drug choices.

cards.f: Describe the classic progression of appendicitis pain.
cards.b: Vague periumbilical pain (visceral, midgut) that migrates to the right iliac fossa as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed, with anorexia and low-grade fever.

cards.f: What is Rovsing's sign?
cards.b: Pain in the right iliac fossa when the left iliac fossa is pressed, suggesting appendicitis.

cards.f: What are the revised Atlanta (2012) criteria for diagnosing acute pancreatitis?
cards.b: Two of three: characteristic abdominal pain; serum amylase or lipase at least 3 times the upper limit of normal; characteristic imaging findings.

cards.f: What does PANCREAS stand for in the Glasgow–Imrie score?
cards.b: PaO₂ <8 kPa, Age >55, Neutrophils (WCC) >15, Calcium <2, Renal (urea >16), Enzymes (LDH >600 or AST >200), Albumin <32, Sugar (glucose >10). Three or more within 48 hours suggests severe pancreatitis.

cards.f: Are prophylactic antibiotics recommended in acute pancreatitis?
cards.b: No; antibiotics are reserved for confirmed or strongly suspected infection, such as infected necrosis or cholangitis.

cards.f: State Charcot's triad and Reynolds' pentad.
cards.b: Charcot's triad: fever, jaundice and RUQ pain (ascending cholangitis). Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension and confusion, indicating severe suppurative cholangitis.

cards.f: When should cholecystectomy be performed for acute cholecystitis (NICE CG188)?
cards.b: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy within one week of diagnosis.

cards.f: What is the 3-6-9 rule on abdominal imaging?
cards.b: Upper limits of normal diameter: small bowel 3 cm, colon 6 cm, caecum 9 cm.

cards.f: What clue suggests acute mesenteric ischaemia?
cards.b: Severe pain out of proportion to abdominal signs, often in a patient with AF or vascular disease, with a raised lactate; confirm with CT angiography.

cards.f: Why is a closed-loop large-bowel obstruction dangerous?
cards.b: A competent ileocaecal valve prevents decompression into the small bowel, so the caecum distends progressively and can perforate.

cards.f: Which operation is used for a caecal or ascending colon cancer?
cards.b: Right hemicolectomy.

cards.f: What is a Hartmann's procedure?
cards.b: Resection of the sigmoid colon with an end colostomy and closure of the rectal stump, usually as an emergency for perforation or obstruction.

cards.f: When is an abdominoperineal resection needed?
cards.b: For low rectal cancers involving or very close to the anal sphincters; it leaves a permanent end colostomy.

cards.f: How do you distinguish an ileostomy from a colostomy on examination?
cards.b: An ileostomy is spouted (to protect skin from irritant output) and usually in the right iliac fossa; a colostomy is flush and usually in the left iliac fossa.

cards.f: What FIT result prompts suspected colorectal cancer referral in primary care?
cards.b: 10 µg haemoglobin per gram of faeces or above (NICE DG56, 2023). This is far lower than the screening programme threshold (120 µg Hb/g in England, being lowered to 80).

cards.f: How does an indirect inguinal hernia differ anatomically from a direct one?
cards.b: An indirect hernia passes through the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; a direct hernia pushes through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to them.

cards.f: How are femoral and inguinal hernias distinguished clinically?
cards.b: Inguinal hernias emerge above and medial to the pubic tubercle; femoral hernias emerge below and lateral to it.

cards.f: Why should femoral hernias be repaired promptly?
cards.b: The femoral canal has a narrow, rigid neck, so the risk of incarceration and strangulation is high.

cards.f: Contrast oesophageal adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma.
cards.b: Adenocarcinoma: lower third, associated with reflux, Barrett's and obesity, now commonest in the UK. SCC: upper and middle thirds, associated with smoking and alcohol.

cards.f: Where are most anal fissures and what do off-midline fissures suggest?
cards.b: Posterior midline; off-midline or multiple fissures suggest Crohn's disease, infection or malignancy.

cards.f: What is total mesorectal excision?
cards.b: Excision of the rectum within its intact mesorectal fascial envelope, used in rectal cancer surgery to reduce local recurrence.

cards.f: How is the ABPI calculated?
cards.b: Highest ankle systolic pressure divided by highest brachial systolic pressure.

cards.f: How is ABPI interpreted?
cards.b: Below 0.9 indicates PAD and below about 0.5 indicates severe disease; above about 1.3–1.4 suggests incompressible calcified vessels.

cards.f: What are the 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia?
cards.b: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishing cold, paraesthesia and paralysis.

cards.f: How do embolic and thrombotic acute limb ischaemia differ?
cards.b: Embolism is sudden, often from AF, with no prior claudication and normal contralateral pulses; thrombosis occurs on existing disease with prior claudication and collaterals, so onset may be less abrupt.

cards.f: Who is offered AAA screening in England?
cards.b: Men in the year they turn 65, with a one-off abdominal ultrasound; older men can self-refer.

cards.f: What are the AAA surveillance intervals?
cards.b: 3.0–4.4 cm: yearly scans; 4.5–5.4 cm: three-monthly scans; 5.5 cm or more, rapid growth over 1 cm a year or symptoms: refer to vascular service within 2 weeks.

cards.f: What is permissive hypotension in ruptured AAA?
cards.b: Limiting fluid resuscitation to keep the patient conscious with a lower-than-normal BP, avoiding clot disruption and dilutional coagulopathy before repair.

cards.f: When is carotid endarterectomy indicated after TIA or minor stroke?
cards.b: For symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50–99% by NASCET criteria, with urgent referral and surgery ideally within 2 weeks of symptoms.

cards.f: What is the first-line treatment for symptomatic truncal varicose veins (NICE CG168)?
cards.b: Endothermal ablation (radiofrequency or endovenous laser), followed by foam sclerotherapy and then surgery if unsuitable.

cards.f: Why must ABPI be checked before compression therapy for a leg ulcer?
cards.b: Compression can cause pressure necrosis and limb ischaemia if significant arterial disease is present.

cards.f: Which complication follows revascularisation of an acutely ischaemic limb?
cards.b: Reperfusion injury with compartment syndrome needing fasciotomy, plus hyperkalaemia, acidosis and myoglobinuric AKI.

cards.f: What is first-line analgesia for renal colic (NICE NG118)?
cards.b: An NSAID by any route, unless contraindicated.

cards.f: What is the first-line imaging for suspected renal colic in adults?
cards.b: Low-dose non-contrast CT KUB within 24 hours of presentation; ultrasound is used in pregnancy and children.

cards.f: Why is an obstructed infected kidney an emergency?
cards.b: Pus under pressure leads rapidly to sepsis and renal loss; it needs antibiotics and urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent.

cards.f: List the clinical features of testicular torsion.
cards.b: Sudden severe testicular pain with nausea or vomiting, a high-riding testis with a horizontal lie, and an absent cremasteric reflex.

cards.f: What is the management of suspected testicular torsion?
cards.b: Immediate scrotal exploration without waiting for imaging, ideally within 6 hours, with fixation of both testes.

cards.f: How do alpha-blockers and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors differ in BPH?
cards.b: Alpha-blockers relax prostatic smooth muscle and act within days; 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors shrink the prostate over months and reduce the risk of retention and surgery.

cards.f: What effect do 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors have on PSA?
cards.b: They roughly halve PSA, which must be taken into account when interpreting results.

cards.f: What is the first-line investigation for suspected localised prostate cancer (NICE NG131)?
cards.b: Multiparametric MRI, before biopsy.

cards.f: Which tumour markers are used in testicular cancer?
cards.b: AFP, β-hCG and LDH; AFP is not raised in pure seminoma.

cards.f: Why is a testicular tumour removed through an inguinal incision?
cards.b: Radical inguinal orchidectomy avoids scrotal violation, which could seed tumour into scrotal lymphatic drainage.

cards.f: What is the main risk factor for bladder cancer and its classic presentation?
cards.b: Smoking (also occupational aromatic amines); painless visible haematuria.

cards.f: What does triple assessment of a breast lump involve?
cards.b: Clinical examination, imaging (mammography and/or ultrasound by age) and pathology (core needle biopsy).

cards.f: Who is invited for NHS breast screening?
cards.b: Women from age 50 up to their 71st birthday, every three years, by mammography.

cards.f: Why is ultrasound preferred to mammography in younger women?
cards.b: Younger breast tissue is denser, which reduces mammographic sensitivity.

cards.f: What is the typical presentation of a fibroadenoma?
cards.b: A smooth, firm, highly mobile painless lump in a young woman.

cards.f: How is a lactational breast abscess managed?
cards.b: Ultrasound-guided aspiration or drainage plus antibiotics active against Staphylococcus aureus, with continued breastfeeding or expressing.

cards.f: What causes single-duct bloody nipple discharge most often?
cards.b: Intraductal papilloma, although carcinoma must be excluded.

cards.f: What is DCIS?
cards.b: Ductal carcinoma in situ: malignant epithelial cells confined within the ducts, without invasion through the basement membrane, often detected as microcalcification on screening.

cards.f: How is the axilla staged in clinically node-negative breast cancer?
cards.b: Sentinel lymph node biopsy, after a normal axillary ultrasound.

cards.f: Compare tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors.
cards.b: Tamoxifen is a SERM used in pre- and postmenopausal women, with VTE and endometrial cancer risks; aromatase inhibitors block peripheral oestrogen synthesis, are used after menopause and cause bone loss and arthralgia.

cards.f: What adverse effect must be monitored with trastuzumab?
cards.b: Cardiotoxicity (reduced LVEF), so cardiac function is monitored by echocardiography or MUGA.

cards.f: Calculate the NPI for a 2 cm, grade 3 tumour with no nodal involvement.
What does <C>ABCDE mean in trauma?
cards.b: Catastrophic haemorrhage control first, then airway with cervical spine protection, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure.

cards.f: What are the key immediate steps for an open fracture (BOAST 2017)?
cards.b: IV antibiotics within 1 hour, photograph the wound, saline-soaked dressing, splintage, neurovascular check, tetanus cover and timely surgical debridement.

cards.f: How is a displaced intracapsular hip fracture managed (NICE CG124)?
cards.b: Arthroplasty: total hip replacement if previously independent outdoors with no more than a stick, not cognitively impaired and medically fit; otherwise hemiarthroplasty.

cards.f: Which implant is used for an extracapsular trochanteric hip fracture?
cards.b: A sliding hip screw; subtrochanteric fractures are treated with an intramedullary nail.

cards.f: Why are displaced intracapsular hip fractures prone to avascular necrosis?
cards.b: The femoral head is supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, which run along the neck and are disrupted by displacement.

cards.f: Why is a suspected scaphoid fracture treated even with a normal X-ray?
cards.b: Early X-rays often miss it, and the retrograde blood supply puts the proximal pole at risk of avascular necrosis and non-union; immobilise and arrange MRI.

cards.f: What are the early signs of compartment syndrome?
cards.b: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the compartment's muscles; pulses are often preserved until late.

cards.f: What are the red flags of cauda equina syndrome?
cards.b: Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, faecal incontinence and sexual dysfunction; needs emergency MRI.

cards.f: State the Ottawa ankle rules.
cards.b: X-ray if malleolar pain plus bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to bear weight both immediately after injury and in the department.

cards.f: Describe Salter–Harris types I–V.
cards.b: I through the physis; II physis and metaphysis (commonest); III physis and epiphysis; IV through metaphysis, physis and epiphysis; V crush injury to the physis.

cards.f: Which nerve should be checked after anterior shoulder dislocation?
cards.b: The axillary nerve, by testing sensation over the lateral upper arm ('regimental badge' area) and deltoid function.

cards.f: What is the triad of general anaesthesia?
cards.b: Hypnosis, analgesia and muscle relaxation.

cards.f: What is the mechanism of propofol and its main cardiovascular effect?
cards.b: It potentiates GABA-A receptors; it causes vasodilatation and hypotension.

cards.f: Why is ketamine useful in haemodynamically unstable patients?
cards.b: As an NMDA antagonist it maintains sympathetic tone and blood pressure, preserves airway reflexes and bronchodilates, while also providing analgesia.

cards.f: Define minimum alveolar concentration (MAC).
cards.b: The alveolar concentration of an inhaled anaesthetic that prevents movement in response to surgical incision in 50% of patients; lower MAC means higher potency.

cards.f: Give three contraindications to suxamethonium.
cards.b: Hyperkalaemia or risk of it (burns after the first day, crush injury, denervation such as spinal cord injury), personal or family history of malignant hyperthermia, and known pseudocholinesterase deficiency.

cards.f: How does sugammadex work?
cards.b: It encapsulates the steroidal neuromuscular blockers rocuronium and vecuronium, reversing blockade without anticholinesterase side effects.

cards.f: Why is glycopyrronium given with neostigmine?
cards.b: Neostigmine increases acetylcholine at muscarinic as well as nicotinic receptors; glycopyrronium blocks the muscarinic effects such as bradycardia and secretions.

cards.f: What are the features and treatment of malignant hyperthermia?
cards.b: Rising end-tidal CO₂, tachycardia, rigidity, hyperthermia, acidosis and hyperkalaemia after volatile agents or suxamethonium; stop triggers, cool and give dantrolene.

cards.f: What are the signs and treatment of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity?
cards.b: Perioral tingling, tinnitus, agitation, seizures and arrhythmias or cardiac arrest; stop injecting, support ABC, treat seizures and give lipid emulsion.

cards.f: How does spinal anaesthesia differ from epidural?
cards.b: Spinal is a single injection into the subarachnoid space giving a quick, dense block; epidural uses a catheter in the epidural space giving a slower, titratable block for prolonged analgesia.

cards.f: What are the four Apfel risk factors for PONV?
cards.b: Female sex, non-smoker, history of PONV or motion sickness, and postoperative opioid use.

cards.f: What did NAP6 (2018) find were the commonest causes of perioperative anaphylaxis?
cards.b: Antibiotics, followed by neuromuscular blocking agents, chlorhexidine and patent blue dye.

cards.f: What is the only reliable confirmation of tracheal intubation?
cards.b: A sustained waveform capnography trace; 'no trace = wrong place' (NAP4, 2011).

questions.q: At which point of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist does the team confirm patient identity, procedure and site immediately before skin incision?
questions.why: The time out happens before skin incision, when the whole team confirms patient, procedure and site.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman has fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. BP 86/50 and she is confused. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Charcot's triad plus hypotension and confusion forms Reynolds' pentad, indicating severe ascending cholangitis needing antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage.

questions.q: A hernia is reduced, and pressure over the midpoint of the inguinal ligament (deep ring) controls it when the patient coughs. What type of hernia is this?
questions.why: Control by pressure over the deep ring suggests an indirect hernia, which travels through the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; clinical distinction is imperfect, however.

questions.q: A man's ankle systolic pressures are 92 and 84 mmHg, and his brachial pressures are 132 and 128 mmHg. What is his ABPI (to 2 decimal places)?
questions.why: ABPI uses the highest ankle pressure over the highest brachial pressure: 92 ÷ 132 = 0.70, consistent with moderate PAD.

questions.q: A 72-year-old man on AAA surveillance has an aneurysm measuring 5.0 cm, which measured 3.8 cm 12 months ago. He is asymptomatic. What is the correct action?
options: Refer to the vascular service to be seen within 2 weeks
questions.why: Growth of more than 1 cm in a year (1.2 cm here) is an indication for vascular referral even though the diameter is below 5.5 cm.

questions.q: What is the first-line imaging test for a non-pregnant adult with suspected renal colic?
questions.why: NICE NG118 recommends low-dose non-contrast CT KUB within 24 hours; ultrasound is first-line in pregnancy and children.

questions.q: A 23-year-old woman has a 1.5 cm smooth, highly mobile, painless breast lump. What is the most appropriate first imaging test as part of triple assessment?
questions.why: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality in young women because dense breast tissue reduces mammographic sensitivity.

questions.q: An 81-year-old who walks outdoors independently without aids, has no cognitive impairment and is medically fit sustains a displaced intracapsular hip fracture. What is the recommended operation?
questions.why: NICE CG124 recommends total hip replacement for displaced intracapsular fractures in people who were independent outdoors with no more than a stick, are not cognitively impaired and are medically fit.

questions.q: Which drug reverses rocuronium by encapsulation?
questions.why: Sugammadex is a modified cyclodextrin that encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium; neostigmine works by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase.

questions.q: During a sevoflurane anaesthetic, a patient develops a rising end-tidal CO₂ despite increased ventilation, tachycardia, masseter rigidity and a rising temperature. What is the specific treatment?
questions.why: This is malignant hyperthermia; stop the volatile agent and give dantrolene, which reduces calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

questions.q: A 66-year-old with type 2 diabetes on metformin, gliclazide and dapagliflozin is listed for an elective hemicolectomy. Outline four key points in managing her diabetes perioperatively.
markScheme: Follow CPOC guidance with early preoperative HbA1c check and optimisation
Omit dapagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor) the day before and the day of surgery due to euglycaemic DKA risk
Omit the sulfonylurea while fasting to avoid hypoglycaemia; review metformin according to missed meals and renal function/contrast
Variable-rate IV insulin infusion if more than one meal will be missed or control is poor; first on the list, regular glucose monitoring, check ketones
questions.modelAnswer: Perioperative diabetes care follows CPOC guidance. HbA1c should be checked at referral so that poor control can be optimised before surgery. Dapagliflozin is omitted the day before and the day of surgery because of the risk of euglycaemic ketoacidosis, and blood ketones should be checked if she becomes unwell. Gliclazide is omitted while she is fasting to avoid hypoglycaemia, and metformin is reviewed according to the number of missed meals and her renal function. Because a hemicolectomy usually means more than one missed meal, she is likely to need a variable-rate insulin infusion, ideally with a slot early on the list.

questions.q: List three features in a woman of reproductive age with right iliac fossa pain that make ectopic pregnancy more likely than appendicitis.
markScheme: Positive pregnancy test with missed period or amenorrhoea
Vaginal bleeding or brownish discharge, shoulder-tip pain (diaphragmatic irritation) or cervical motion tenderness
Risk factors: previous ectopic, pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal surgery, IUD or assisted conception
questions.modelAnswer: A positive pregnancy test is essential and, with amenorrhoea, makes ectopic pregnancy the key diagnosis to exclude. Vaginal bleeding, shoulder-tip pain from blood irritating the diaphragm and cervical motion tenderness all point towards a gynaecological cause. Risk factors such as previous ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal surgery, an intrauterine device or assisted conception increase the likelihood further.

questions.q: A 72-year-old with no previous surgery presents with 2 days of colicky abdominal pain, distension and absolute constipation. CT shows a dilated colon to 8 cm with a caecum of 11 cm and an obstructing sigmoid lesion. The ileocaecal valve is competent. Explain the significance and outline management.
markScheme: Large-bowel obstruction, likely from sigmoid carcinoma
Competent ileocaecal valve creates a closed loop; caecum above 9 cm risks ischaemia and perforation
Resuscitate: IV fluids, NG tube if vomiting, catheter, analgesia, bloods including lactate
Urgent senior surgical review; signs of peritonitis or caecal tenderness mean emergency surgery
Options: emergency resection (e.g. Hartmann's) or stenting as a bridge or palliation in selected cases; staging and MDT
questions.modelAnswer: This is large-bowel obstruction, probably due to a sigmoid carcinoma. Because the ileocaecal valve is competent, gas cannot decompress into the small bowel, creating a closed loop. The caecum, at 11 cm, is above the 9 cm limit and is at risk of ischaemia and perforation. She needs resuscitation with IV fluids, analgesia, catheterisation, an NG tube if vomiting and bloods including lactate. Senior surgical review is needed urgently; caecal tenderness or peritonism demands emergency surgery, usually a Hartmann's procedure. Colonic stenting may be an option as a bridge to surgery or for palliation, with MDT discussion and full staging.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man has a 3 cm adenocarcinoma 8 cm from the anal verge on colonoscopy. Name the investigations needed for staging and the likely operation.
markScheme: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for distant metastases
Pelvic MRI for local staging (circumferential resection margin, nodes, extramural vascular invasion)
CEA baseline and MDT discussion (neoadjuvant therapy if high risk)
Low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision, often with a defunctioning loop ileostomy
questions.modelAnswer: Rectal cancer staging needs CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to look for liver and lung metastases, and pelvic MRI to define local stage, nodal involvement, extramural venous invasion and threat to the circumferential resection margin. A baseline CEA is useful for follow-up. The case should be discussed by the colorectal MDT, which may recommend neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced disease. A mid-rectal tumour at 8 cm is usually treated with a low anterior resection and total mesorectal excision, typically with a temporary defunctioning loop ileostomy.

questions.q: A 70-year-old woman in AF presents with a 3-hour history of a cold, pale, painful right leg with no pulses below the femoral and reduced sensation. Outline your immediate management.
markScheme: Recognise acute limb ischaemia, likely embolic from AF; sensory loss means the limb is threatened
IV unfractionated heparin immediately (unless contraindicated) and analgesia
Urgent vascular surgical review; imaging (CT angiography) only if it does not delay revascularisation
Emergency revascularisation (embolectomy); after reperfusion monitor for compartment syndrome and hyperkalaemia
questions.modelAnswer: This is acute limb ischaemia, probably embolic from atrial fibrillation given the sudden onset. Sensory loss means the limb is immediately threatened. She needs IV unfractionated heparin to prevent clot propagation, adequate analgesia and an immediate vascular surgical review. Imaging such as CT angiography is used only if it will not delay treatment. Emergency embolectomy is the usual approach. After reperfusion, she must be monitored for compartment syndrome needing fasciotomy, and for hyperkalaemia, acidosis and AKI. Long-term anticoagulation for AF is then needed.

questions.q: Give three indications for urgent intervention (rather than conservative management) in a patient with a ureteric stone.
markScheme: Infection or sepsis with obstruction (obstructed infected kidney)
Uncontrollable pain despite adequate analgesia
AKI, obstruction of a solitary or transplanted kidney, or bilateral obstruction
questions.modelAnswer: Urgent decompression or stone removal is needed when infection complicates obstruction, because an obstructed infected kidney can rapidly cause sepsis. Other indications include pain that cannot be controlled with adequate analgesia, and obstruction causing AKI, especially in a solitary or transplanted kidney or in bilateral obstruction.

questions.q: A 46-year-old woman has a 2.8 cm grade 2 invasive ductal carcinoma, ER-positive and HER2-negative, with one positive axillary node. Calculate her NPI and state two adjuvant treatments.
markScheme: Adjuvant endocrine therapy appropriate to menopausal status (tamoxifen if premenopausal)
Radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery and/or chemotherapy according to risk; HER2-targeted therapy not indicated
questions.modelAnswer: Her Nottingham Prognostic Index is (0.2 × 2.8) + grade 2 + nodal score 2 (one to three nodes) = 0.56 + 4 = 4.56. Because the tumour is ER-positive, she needs adjuvant endocrine therapy; at 46 she is likely premenopausal, so tamoxifen would usually be used, sometimes with ovarian suppression. After breast-conserving surgery she needs whole-breast radiotherapy, and adjuvant chemotherapy may be offered depending on her overall risk. Trastuzumab is not indicated because the tumour is HER2-negative.

questions.q: Using the Ottawa ankle rules, list three findings that indicate an ankle X-ray is needed.
markScheme: Bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus
Bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the medial malleolus
Inability to bear weight (four steps) both immediately after injury and in the emergency department
questions.modelAnswer: With pain in the malleolar zone, an ankle X-ray is needed if there is bone tenderness along the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus, or along the posterior edge or tip of the medial malleolus, or if the patient was unable to bear weight for four steps both immediately after the injury and when examined in the department.

questions.q: A 24-year-old has a tibial shaft fracture treated with an intramedullary nail. Six hours later he has severe pain despite opioids, pain on passive toe extension, and a tense calf; foot pulses are palpable. Explain the diagnosis, pathophysiology and management.
markScheme: Acute compartment syndrome
Raised pressure within a closed fascial compartment exceeds capillary perfusion pressure, causing ischaemia
Palpable pulses do not exclude it, because arterial pressure exceeds compartment pressure until late
Remove constricting dressings to skin, keep the limb at heart level (do not elevate), urgent senior review; pressure measurement if diagnosis unclear
Emergency fasciotomy of all four leg compartments; monitor for rhabdomyolysis and AKI
questions.modelAnswer: This is acute compartment syndrome, a classic complication of tibial fractures and nailing. Bleeding and oedema raise the pressure within a closed fascial compartment until it exceeds capillary perfusion pressure, causing muscle and nerve ischaemia. Pulses remain palpable because arterial pressure is much higher than compartment pressure, so their presence is not reassuring. Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are the earliest signs. Dressings should be released to the skin and the limb kept at heart level, with immediate senior orthopaedic review; compartment pressures can be measured if the picture is unclear. Treatment is emergency four-compartment fasciotomy, with monitoring for rhabdomyolysis and AKI.

questions.q: Explain why a rapid sequence induction is used for an emergency laparotomy for bowel obstruction, and list its key steps.
markScheme: High risk of regurgitation and aspiration of gastric contents (full stomach, obstruction)
NG aspiration and adequate preoxygenation before induction
Induction agent and rapid-onset neuromuscular blocker given in quick succession, with or without cricoid pressure, avoiding mask ventilation where possible
Intubation with a cuffed tube and confirmation by waveform capnography
questions.modelAnswer: Patients with bowel obstruction have a full stomach and raised intra-abdominal pressure, so the risk of regurgitation and aspiration at induction is high. The stomach is decompressed with an NG tube beforehand, and the patient is preoxygenated to extend the safe apnoea time. An induction agent and a fast-acting neuromuscular blocker are given in quick succession, with or without cricoid pressure, minimising mask ventilation. A cuffed tracheal tube is placed to protect the airway, and correct placement is confirmed with waveform capnography.

questions.q: Mr Lewis, 71, is day 3 after an elective open right hemicolectomy. He becomes acutely breathless with pleuritic chest pain. RR 26, HR 118, BP 112/70, SpO₂ 89% on air, temperature 37.6 °C. His calf is not swollen. He is on LMWH prophylaxis and anti-embolism stockings but has mobilised only to the chair. His abdomen is soft with appropriate wound tenderness. Discuss the differential diagnosis, investigations and management.
markScheme: Differentials: PE, hospital-acquired pneumonia/aspiration, atelectasis, MI, pulmonary oedema/fluid overload, anastomotic leak with sepsis
ABCDE; oxygen to 94–98%; call for senior help
Investigations: ABG, ECG, CXR, FBC, U&E, CRP, troponin, cultures if febrile
Wells score: PE likely given tachycardia and recent surgery; D-dimer unhelpful postoperatively
CTPA (renal function permitting); leg Doppler if CTPA contraindicated
Anticoagulation: weigh postoperative bleeding risk with surgical team; consider UFH (reversible) if bleeding risk high
Massive PE with hypotension: thrombolysis relatively contraindicated after major surgery; consider catheter-directed therapy/embolectomy
If pneumonia: hospital-acquired antibiotics per policy, physio
Review VTE prophylaxis adequacy and duration (extended after cancer surgery)
Communicate with surgical team and patient; document
questions.modelAnswer:
Sudden breathlessness with pleuritic pain, tachycardia and hypoxia three days after major abdominal surgery is a pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise. The differential includes hospital-acquired pneumonia or aspiration, atelectasis, myocardial infarction, fluid overload with pulmonary oedema and, importantly, sepsis from an anastomotic leak, which often presents with tachycardia and respiratory signs.

He should be assessed with an ABCDE approach and given oxygen to target 94–98%, with early senior help. Initial investigations include an arterial blood gas, ECG (sinus tachycardia is commonest in PE; also look for ischaemia or right heart strain), chest X-ray, FBC, renal function, CRP, troponin and blood cultures if febrile. His Wells score is above 4 because of heart rate over 100 and surgery within four weeks, with PE as the most likely diagnosis, so PE is "likely". A D-dimer would be unhelpful because it is almost always raised after surgery. He should have a CT pulmonary angiogram, checking renal function first. If CTPA cannot be done, leg Doppler or V/Q imaging may help.

If PE is confirmed, anticoagulation must be balanced against postoperative bleeding risk and discussed with the surgical team. Unfractionated heparin may be preferred early on because it is short-acting and reversible, before switching to longer-term treatment. If he develops massive PE with hypotension, systemic thrombolysis is relatively contraindicated after recent major surgery, so catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy should be discussed with specialists. If imaging instead shows pneumonia, he needs antibiotics according to local hospital-acquired pneumonia policy, chest physiotherapy and early mobilisation. If the abdomen is tender or he deteriorates, CT abdomen should look for a leak.

The episode should prompt review of his VTE prophylaxis, including whether extended prophylaxis after cancer surgery had been prescribed. The surgical team, the patient and his family should be kept informed, and the event documented and reviewed.

questions.q: Essay: "Enhanced recovery after surgery is a bundle of common sense that has transformed outcomes." Critically evaluate this statement with reference to the physiological rationale, components and limitations of ERAS.
markScheme: Defines ERAS: multimodal, evidence-based perioperative pathway to reduce surgical stress response
Physiological rationale: stress response, insulin resistance, catabolism, ileus, immobility
Preoperative components: education, prehabilitation, optimisation, carbohydrate loading, minimal fasting
Intraoperative: minimally invasive surgery, goal-directed fluids, avoiding drains/NG tubes, normothermia, regional anaesthesia
Postoperative: early feeding, early mobilisation, opioid-sparing analgesia, early catheter removal, PONV prophylaxis
Evidence: shorter length of stay and fewer complications in colorectal surgery; no increase in readmission
Critique: 'common sense' understates evidence and change management; elements individually small
Compliance-outcome relationship: benefits depend on high adherence and audit
Limitations: emergency and frail patients, heterogeneous trials, length of stay as a surrogate
Balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) is a multimodal, evidence-based perioperative pathway designed to reduce the physiological stress of surgery and speed functional recovery. It began in colorectal surgery and has since spread to most specialties.

The rationale is physiological. Surgery triggers a neuroendocrine and inflammatory stress response, causing insulin resistance, protein catabolism, fluid shifts, ileus and immunosuppression. Traditional practice made this worse through prolonged fasting, routine nasogastric tubes and drains, large volumes of IV fluid, opioid-heavy analgesia and enforced bed rest. ERAS removes or reverses these. Preoperatively it includes patient education, optimisation of anaemia and comorbidity, prehabilitation, short fasting and carbohydrate loading to reduce insulin resistance. Intraoperatively it uses minimally invasive surgery, goal-directed fluid therapy, normothermia, regional techniques and avoidance of routine drains and tubes. Postoperatively it emphasises early oral feeding, early mobilisation, early catheter removal, PONV prophylaxis and opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia.

The statement is partly right. Many components appear intuitive, and trials and meta-analyses in elective colorectal surgery consistently show shorter hospital stays and fewer complications without more readmissions. However, calling it "common sense" undersells two points. First, several elements overturned entrenched dogma, such as feeding after bowel anastomosis and avoiding NG tubes, and needed evidence to change practice. Second, the benefit comes from the bundle and from high adherence. Outcomes improve as compliance rises, which requires multidisciplinary teams, audit and organisational change rather than simple intuition.

There are real limitations. Much of the evidence comes from elective, relatively fit patients; applying ERAS to emergency laparotomy, frail older people or complex cancer surgery is harder, and the evidence is weaker. Trials are heterogeneous, the contribution of individual elements is uncertain, and length of stay is a surrogate that can be influenced by discharge pressures rather than true recovery. Patient-reported outcomes and long-term function are less studied.

In conclusion, ERAS has transformed elective surgical care, but it is a structured, evidence-based system that requires sustained implementation, not mere common sense, and its benefits outside elective surgery remain less certain.

questions.q: Mrs Begum, 58, presents with 12 hours of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting. Bloods at 48 hours: WCC 17 × 10⁹/L, glucose 9.2 mmol/L, urea 18 mmol/L, calcium 1.9 mmol/L, albumin 30 g/L, LDH 450 U/L, AST 160 U/L, PaO₂ 9.5 kPa. Lipase was 6 times the upper limit of normal and ultrasound shows gallstones. Calculate her Glasgow–Imrie score and describe management.
markScheme: Diagnosis: acute gallstone pancreatitis (pain plus lipase >3× ULN)
Scores: age >55 (1), WCC >15 (1), urea >16 (1), calcium <2 (1), albumin <32 (1)
PaO₂ ≥8 (0), glucose ≤10 (0), LDH ≤600 and AST ≤200 (0): total 5
Score ≥3 predicts severe pancreatitis; HDU/critical care review
IV fluid resuscitation with careful monitoring (avoid overload); catheter and urine output
Analgesia, antiemetics, oxygen as needed; early enteral nutrition (NG/NJ if needed)
No routine prophylactic antibiotics; treat confirmed infection
Urgent ERCP only if cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction
CT after 72 hours if deteriorating to assess necrosis/collections
Cholecystectomy once recovered (same admission in mild disease; delayed in severe with collections)
questions.modelAnswer:
Mrs Begum has acute pancreatitis: typical pain plus a lipase more than three times the upper limit of normal meets the revised Atlanta criteria. Gallstones on ultrasound suggest a biliary cause.

Her Glasgow–Imrie (PANCREAS) score is: PaO₂ 9.5 kPa (not below 8, 0); age 58 (over 55, 1); WCC 17 (over 15, 1); calcium 1.9 (below 2, 1); urea 18 (over 16, 1); enzymes LDH 450 and AST 160 (below 600 and 200, 0); albumin 30 (below 32, 1); glucose 9.2 (not over 10, 0). Her total is 5. A score of 3 or more within 48 hours predicts severe pancreatitis, so she should be reviewed by critical care and managed in a high-dependency setting.

Management is mainly supportive. She needs IV crystalloid resuscitation guided by heart rate, blood pressure and urine output, with a catheter and strict fluid balance; aggressive over-resuscitation is avoided because it can cause fluid overload and abdominal compartment syndrome. Adequate analgesia, antiemetics and oxygen to target are needed. Early enteral nutrition, orally or by NG or nasojejunal tube if needed, helps maintain the gut barrier and is preferred to parenteral feeding. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended; antibiotics are reserved for confirmed infection such as cholangitis or infected necrosis. Urgent ERCP is indicated only if she has cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction, not for all gallstone pancreatitis.

If she fails to improve or deteriorates, contrast-enhanced CT after about 72 hours assesses necrosis and collections, which are managed by a specialist pancreatic team, with a step-up approach to drainage if infected. Complications to monitor include ARDS, AKI, hypocalcaemia, hyperglycaemia, pseudocyst and splenic vein thrombosis.

To prevent recurrence, she needs cholecystectomy. In mild gallstone pancreatitis this is done during the same admission; in severe disease with collections it is delayed until inflammation settles. ERCP with sphincterotomy is an alternative if she is unfit for surgery.

questions.q: Essay: "In the modern era, imaging has made clinical examination of the acute abdomen redundant." Discuss, with reference to specific conditions, the strengths and limitations of clinical assessment and of CT and ultrasound.
markScheme: Clinical assessment identifies peritonism, shock and need for urgent resuscitation/theatre
History patterns (migratory RIF pain, colic, pain out of proportion) shape differential and imaging choice
CT strengths: high accuracy for appendicitis, perforation, obstruction, diverticulitis, AAA, mesenteric ischaemia
CT limitations: radiation (young, pregnancy), contrast nephropathy concerns, delay, incidental findings, availability
Ultrasound strengths: biliary disease, gynaecological pathology, children and pregnancy; no radiation
Ultrasound limitations: operator dependence, body habitus, bowel gas
Conditions where clinical judgement dominates: ruptured AAA in unstable patient, testicular torsion, ectopic with shock
Mesenteric ischaemia shows dangers of reassurance from soft abdomen
Risk scores (Alvarado, AIR) combine clinical data to target imaging
Conclusion: examination and imaging complementary; examination triages and interprets
questions.modelAnswer:
Cross-sectional imaging has changed emergency surgery. CT abdomen and pelvis is highly accurate for appendicitis, perforation, bowel obstruction, diverticulitis and many other pathologies, and negative appendicectomy rates have fallen where it is widely used. Yet the claim that clinical examination is redundant does not survive scrutiny.

First, clinical assessment decides who needs imaging, how urgently, and whether imaging is safe at all. A patient with a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm who is hypotensive should go straight to theatre or an endovascular suite rather than to the CT scanner. A woman with a positive pregnancy test, abdominal pain and shock may have a ruptured ectopic pregnancy and needs immediate gynaecological surgery. Testicular torsion, which can present as lower abdominal pain in boys, is a clinical diagnosis where imaging only costs salvage time. Peritonism, a rigid abdomen or signs of shock identify patients who need resuscitation and theatre regardless of the scan.

Second, the history and examination shape the differential and therefore the choice of imaging. Classic migratory right iliac fossa pain, Murphy's sign or colicky loin-to-groin pain direct the clinician towards ultrasound, CT or CT KUB. Scores such as Alvarado or the Appendicitis Inflammatory Response score combine clinical findings to target imaging, particularly to avoid irradiating young patients unnecessarily. Ultrasound is the first choice for biliary disease, in children and in pregnancy, but it is operator-dependent and limited by body habitus and bowel gas.

Third, examination has limitations that make imaging essential. Acute mesenteric ischaemia classically causes pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen, so examination can falsely reassure; CT angiography is diagnostic. Elderly, immunosuppressed and obese patients often lack peritoneal signs. Imaging also has costs: radiation, contrast reactions, delay, limited availability out of hours and incidental findings that cause anxiety and further tests.

In conclusion, imaging has refined diagnosis but not replaced examination. The two are complementary. Clinical assessment triages, identifies the unstable patient, selects the right test and interprets its result in context, while imaging adds anatomical precision. A clinician who images without examining risks both delay and error.

questions.q: Mr Shah, 67, has 6 weeks of change in bowel habit to looser stools, intermittent dark red rectal bleeding and 4 kg weight loss. Hb 98 g/L with microcytosis. FIT is 140 µg Hb/g. Colonoscopy shows a sigmoid adenocarcinoma, and CT shows no metastases. He is otherwise fit apart from well-controlled hypertension, and his father had bowel cancer at 70. Discuss the referral pathway, staging, surgical management and follow-up.
markScheme: Meets suspected cancer pathway referral (FIT ≥10, iron deficiency anaemia, change in bowel habit)
Staging: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis; CEA; colonoscopy to assess synchronous lesions
TNM staging and MDT discussion
Optimise preoperatively: treat iron deficiency anaemia (IV iron), prehabilitation, ERAS
Operation: high anterior resection (or sigmoid colectomy), laparoscopic where possible, with lymphadenectomy
Emergency presentation (obstruction/perforation) would favour Hartmann's procedure
Stoma counselling and marking preoperatively
Adjuvant chemotherapy for node-positive (stage III) or high-risk stage II disease
Surveillance: CEA and CT over several years, colonoscopy at intervals
Consider genetic testing (all colorectal cancers tested for Lynch syndrome markers)
questions.modelAnswer:
Mr Shah's symptoms of change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, weight loss and iron-deficiency anaemia, together with a FIT result of 140 µg Hb/g (well above the 10 µg Hb/g threshold), meet the criteria for referral on the suspected lower GI cancer pathway. He has had colonoscopy, which also checks for synchronous tumours and polyps.

Staging is completed with CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, which has excluded distant metastases, and a baseline CEA for later surveillance. The tumour is described using TNM, and the case is discussed at the colorectal multidisciplinary team meeting. All colorectal cancers are now tested for mismatch repair deficiency to screen for Lynch syndrome, which matters for his family and for treatment choices.

Before surgery, his anaemia should be corrected, usually with IV iron given the time available, because preoperative anaemia increases transfusion and complications. He should enter an enhanced recovery pathway with prehabilitation, nutritional assessment and education. Stoma counselling and siting by a specialist nurse are advisable even if a stoma is not planned.

For a sigmoid tumour the operation is a high anterior resection (sigmoid colectomy) with ligation of the inferior mesenteric vessels and removal of the draining lymph nodes, performed laparoscopically or robotically where possible. Primary anastomosis is usual in the elective setting. If he had presented as an emergency with obstruction or perforation, a Hartmann's procedure with an end colostomy would be safer.

The resected specimen provides the pathological stage. Adjuvant chemotherapy is offered for node-positive (stage III) disease and considered in high-risk stage II disease. Follow-up includes regular CEA testing and CT surveillance over the first few years to detect resectable recurrence, especially in the liver, and colonoscopy at intervals to detect metachronous tumours. Lifestyle advice, holistic needs assessment and access to a clinical nurse specialist support his recovery.

questions.q: Mr Evans, 74, collapses at home with sudden severe back and abdominal pain. In ED: HR 130, BP 78/40, pale and clammy, with a tender pulsatile epigastric mass. He has a known 5.2 cm AAA on surveillance. He responds to voice only. Bedside ultrasound confirms the aneurysm. He takes amlodipine and atorvastatin and smoked for 40 years. Discuss the immediate management, the choice of repair and potential complications.
markScheme: Diagnosis: ruptured AAA until proven otherwise
Immediate senior vascular and anaesthetic involvement; activate major haemorrhage protocol
Large-bore access, crossmatch, permissive hypotension (conscious patient, lower target BP)
Avoid excessive crystalloid (dilutional coagulopathy, clot disruption)
CT angiography only if stable enough, to plan EVAR; unstable patient straight to theatre
EVAR vs open repair: anatomy, haemodynamic status, local expertise; NICE NG156 framework
Complications: MI, AKI, colonic ischaemia, abdominal compartment syndrome, limb ischaemia, multi-organ failure
EVAR-specific: endoleak, need for lifelong surveillance
High mortality; discuss goals of care, frailty and patient wishes promptly
Communication with family
questions.modelAnswer:
Sudden back and abdominal pain, collapse and shock in a man with a known AAA is a ruptured aneurysm until proven otherwise. Rupture can occur below the 5.5 cm repair threshold, and mortality is very high.

Immediate management requires simultaneous action. The vascular surgeon, anaesthetist and theatre team should be alerted at once and the major haemorrhage protocol activated. He needs two large-bore cannulae, bloods including crossmatch, clotting and lactate, and blood products in balanced ratios rather than large volumes of crystalloid. Permissive hypotension is used: resuscitate only enough to keep him conscious with a lower-than-normal systolic pressure. Restoring normal pressure risks dislodging the retroperitoneal clot that is containing the rupture, and excess crystalloid causes dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia. Active warming helps limit coagulopathy.

If he remains unstable, he should go directly to theatre or the hybrid suite. If he responds enough, CT angiography establishes whether the aneurysm anatomy is suitable for endovascular repair. EVAR avoids a laparotomy and aortic cross-clamping, and in many centres is preferred for anatomically suitable ruptured aneurysms. NICE NG156 sets out when EVAR or open repair should be considered, taking account of anatomy, age, sex and fitness. Open repair is needed when anatomy is unsuitable or EVAR is unavailable. Frailty, comorbidity and the patient's wishes should be discussed early, as some patients may choose palliation.

Complications after either repair include myocardial infarction, AKI, colonic ischaemia (particularly of the sigmoid when the inferior mesenteric artery is sacrificed, presenting with bloody diarrhoea), abdominal compartment syndrome from retroperitoneal haematoma and bowel oedema, lower limb ischaemia from emboli, respiratory failure and multi-organ failure. After EVAR, endoleaks and graft migration require lifelong imaging surveillance. His family should be kept informed throughout, and his case should prompt review of surveillance practices.

questions.q: Mr Thompson, 76, presents with inability to pass urine for 14 hours and suprapubic pain. He has had 2 years of poor stream, hesitancy and nocturia. He recently started an anticholinergic for urgency, and has been constipated. A catheter drains 1,100 mL. He takes amlodipine for hypertension. Creatinine is 128 µmol/L, compared with 90 µmol/L a year ago. Discuss assessment, management and longer-term options.
markScheme: Diagnosis: acute urinary retention on background of BPH-related LUTS
Precipitants: anticholinergic drug, constipation; also infection, alcohol, postoperative
Urethral catheter, document residual volume (large volume suggests possible chronic component)
Monitor for post-obstructive diuresis and check renal function, electrolytes
Urine dip/culture; DRE for prostate size, nodularity; PSA after counselling, interpreting after retention
Stop anticholinergic, treat constipation
Start alpha-blocker before trial without catheter (TWOC) after a few days
If TWOC fails or high-pressure chronic retention with renal impairment: TURP or alternative surgery; long-term catheter/ISC if unfit
5-alpha-reductase inhibitor for enlarged prostate to reduce retention/surgery risk over months
Patient education and follow-up
questions.modelAnswer:
