Mr Thompson has acute urinary retention on a background of voiding symptoms consistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia. Two likely precipitants are present: the newly started anticholinergic drug, which reduces detrusor contraction, and constipation, which compresses the bladder outlet. Other precipitants to consider are infection, alcohol, immobility and surgery.

Catheterisation relieves the pain, and the residual volume must be recorded. A volume of 1,100 mL is large and raises the possibility of a chronic component. If renal function is impaired, this suggests high-pressure chronic retention, which carries a risk of post-obstructive diuresis. He therefore needs U&E, careful fluid balance and observations after catheterisation. A urine sample should be sent for culture. Digital rectal examination assesses prostate size and checks for a hard, irregular gland suggesting cancer. A PSA can be measured after counselling but is falsely raised by retention and catheterisation, so interpretation should be delayed or done cautiously.

The anticholinergic should be stopped and his constipation treated. He should start an alpha-blocker, which relaxes prostatic smooth muscle and improves the chance of a successful trial without catheter. The trial is usually done a few days later. If it succeeds, he continues the alpha-blocker, and if his prostate is enlarged a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor can be added to shrink it over months and reduce the long-term risk of retention and surgery.

If the trial without catheter fails, or if he has high-pressure chronic retention with renal impairment, he should be referred for bladder outlet surgery such as TURP or one of the newer prostate procedures, after urodynamic assessment where appropriate. If he is unfit for surgery, a long-term urethral or suprapubic catheter, or intermittent self-catheterisation if feasible, are the alternatives. He should be taught how to recognise retention and avoid triggering drugs, and his storage symptoms should be managed in a way that takes his retention risk into account.

questions.q: Essay: "PSA testing does more harm than good." Critically evaluate this statement in the context of the UK approach to prostate cancer detection and management.
markScheme: Explains PSA biology: organ-specific, not cancer-specific; raised by BPH, infection, retention, instrumentation, ejaculation
False positives and false negatives; poor specificity
Overdiagnosis of indolent cancers and overtreatment harms (incontinence, erectile dysfunction, bowel effects)
Screening trials: ERSPC showed mortality reduction with large numbers needed to diagnose; PLCO contamination; CAP trial modest/no clear benefit
UK has no national screening programme; informed-choice approach for men who ask
Higher-risk groups: Black men, family history, BRCA2
Mitigation: multiparametric MRI before biopsy reduces unnecessary biopsies and detection of insignificant cancer
Active surveillance reduces overtreatment of low-risk disease
Ongoing research (e.g. TRANSFORM trial) and risk-adapted screening
Balanced conclusion depending on context and pathway
questions.modelAnswer:
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is produced by prostatic epithelium and is organ-specific rather than cancer-specific. It rises with benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, urinary infection, retention, instrumentation and recent ejaculation, while some significant cancers present with a normal PSA. This poor specificity and imperfect sensitivity explain much of the controversy.

The case for harm is serious. Testing asymptomatic men leads many to biopsy because of false-positive results. Traditional transrectal biopsy carried risks of sepsis and bleeding. PSA testing also detects many low-grade cancers that would never have caused symptoms or death, which is overdiagnosis. Historically, many such men were treated with radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy, risking incontinence, erectile dysfunction and bowel problems without benefit. Screening trial evidence is mixed. The European ERSPC trial showed a reduction in prostate cancer mortality, but large numbers of men had to be screened and diagnosed to prevent one death. The American PLCO trial was confounded by high levels of testing in the control group. The UK CAP trial of a single PSA screen showed at best a small effect on prostate cancer mortality. For these reasons, the UK has no national population screening programme (in May 2026 the UK National Screening Committee recommended against screening all men or Black men as a group, recommending only two-yearly PSA screening for men aged 45–61 with a BRCA2 variant and a family history, planned in England from 2027; check the current position); the informed-choice approach allows men aged 50 and over who request a PSA test to have one after balanced counselling.

The statement is less true for the modern pathway. NICE NG131 recommends multiparametric MRI before biopsy, which allows some men to avoid biopsy and reduces detection of insignificant cancers while improving detection of significant ones. Transperineal biopsy has lowered infection risk. Active surveillance is now standard for low-risk disease, which separates diagnosis from overtreatment. Risk is not uniform either: Black men, men with a family history and BRCA2 carriers have higher risk and may benefit more from earlier testing. Large UK trials such as TRANSFORM are evaluating risk-adapted, MRI-based screening.

In conclusion, unselected PSA screening using the old biopsy-and-treat pathway probably caused more harm than good for many men. With MRI triage, safer biopsy, active surveillance and targeting of higher-risk groups, the balance is shifting. PSA testing is a tool whose value depends on the pathway built around it.

questions.q: Ms Rossi, 52, attends with a 2 cm hard, irregular lump in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast, with skin tethering. There is a palpable mobile left axillary node. She is perimenopausal, takes no regular medication and has a sister who was diagnosed with breast cancer at 44. She asks whether she will lose her breast. Discuss her assessment pathway, the information needed before treatment, and the treatment options.
markScheme: Meets suspected cancer pathway referral (age ≥30 with unexplained lump)
Triple assessment: clinical, mammography plus ultrasound (breast and axilla), core biopsy
Ultrasound-guided biopsy of suspicious axillary node
Pathology: histological type, grade, ER, PR, HER2 status
Staging imaging if node-positive or locally advanced (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, bone scan) per protocol
MDT discussion, breast care nurse, patient preferences
Surgery: breast-conserving surgery plus radiotherapy vs mastectomy (± reconstruction)
Axilla: proven nodal disease → axillary node clearance or radiotherapy; neoadjuvant chemotherapy may downstage
Systemic therapy by receptor status: endocrine (tamoxifen or AI by menopausal status), trastuzumab for HER2+, chemotherapy
Consider genetic testing if criteria met; support, fertility/menopause issues, bone health
questions.modelAnswer:
Ms Rossi's hard, irregular lump with skin tethering and a palpable axillary node is highly suspicious of breast cancer. She meets the criteria for urgent referral on the suspected breast cancer pathway, as she is over 30 with an unexplained lump.

At the breast clinic she should have triple assessment. A clinician examines both breasts and axillae. Imaging includes bilateral mammography, which is appropriate at 52 and also screens the other breast, plus ultrasound of the breast and axilla. Core needle biopsy of the breast lesion, and an ultrasound-guided biopsy of the suspicious axillary node, provide tissue.

Before treatment, the MDT needs the histological type (most often invasive ductal carcinoma of no special type), grade, and receptor status: oestrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2. Because the axilla is involved, staging imaging, typically CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis with or without a bone scan, is performed to exclude metastatic disease according to local protocol. Genetic testing should be considered if her family history or tumour features meet criteria. A breast care nurse should support her throughout.

Treatment options are discussed at the MDT and with her. Surgically, breast-conserving surgery with whole-breast radiotherapy gives equivalent survival to mastectomy when the tumour can be excised with clear margins and a good cosmetic result. Mastectomy, with immediate or delayed reconstruction, is chosen for larger or multifocal tumours or by patient preference. Because the node is biopsy-proven, the axilla usually needs treatment, by axillary node clearance or axillary radiotherapy, rather than sentinel node biopsy alone. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy may be offered first, particularly for HER2-positive or triple-negative disease, to downstage the breast and axilla.

Systemic treatment depends on receptor status. ER-positive disease needs endocrine therapy: an aromatase inhibitor if she is postmenopausal, with bone density monitoring, or tamoxifen if premenopausal. HER2-positive disease is treated with trastuzumab and chemotherapy, with cardiac monitoring. Chemotherapy is based on overall risk. Survivorship care includes managing menopausal symptoms, bone health and psychological support.

questions.q: Mrs Green, 86, lives alone, walks with a frame indoors and has moderate dementia. She is found on the floor after a fall, with a shortened, externally rotated left leg. X-ray shows a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. She lay on the floor overnight and is more confused than usual. Her daughter holds lasting power of attorney for health and welfare. Outline her management from admission to discharge.
markScheme: Analgesia including fascia iliaca or femoral nerve block early in ED
Assess cause of fall and long lie: AKI, rhabdomyolysis (CK), pressure areas, hypothermia, ECG, infection, delirium
Orthogeriatric involvement from admission; optimise but do not delay surgery unnecessarily
Surgery on the day of or day after admission (NICE CG124)
Cemented hemiarthroplasty (not THR due to dementia and mobility)
Capacity assessment for consent; best-interests decision and family involvement if lacking capacity
VTE prophylaxis, delirium prevention, nutrition, pressure care
Mobilise the day after surgery with physiotherapy
Falls assessment and bone health (osteoporosis treatment)
Discharge planning: OT, social care, rehabilitation setting, advance care planning
questions.modelAnswer:
Mrs Green has a displaced intracapsular hip fracture after a fall. Management follows NICE CG124 and involves orthopaedic and orthogeriatric teams from the start.

In the emergency department she needs prompt analgesia, including a fascia iliaca or femoral nerve block, which reduces opioid requirements and the risk of delirium. Her fall and possible long lie need investigation: ECG, blood tests including renal function and creatine kinase for rhabdomyolysis, glucose, a check for infection and assessment of pressure areas, temperature and hydration. She should be screened for delirium and her baseline cognition documented with collateral history.

Surgery should take place on the day of or the day after admission, with medical problems corrected quickly rather than causing avoidable delay. Because she has moderate dementia and limited mobility, total hip replacement is not indicated. A cemented hemiarthroplasty is appropriate. Her capacity to consent must be assessed; if she lacks capacity, the decision is made in her best interests under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, involving her family or any lasting power of attorney.

Postoperatively she needs VTE prophylaxis, adequate analgesia, delirium prevention (orientation, sleep, hydration, avoiding unnecessary drugs and catheters), nutritional support and pressure care. She should be mobilised by physiotherapists the day after surgery, with weight bearing as tolerated. The orthogeriatric team reviews her medication, falls risk factors such as postural hypotension and sedatives, and bone health, starting osteoporosis treatment with vitamin D and calcium replacement as needed.

Discharge planning starts early. Occupational therapy assesses her home and function, and social care and rehabilitation options are discussed with her and her family, including whether she can return home with support or needs a different setting. Given her age and dementia, conversations about prognosis and advance care planning are appropriate.

questions.q: Essay: Discuss the principles of managing open fractures, with reference to classification, the evidence behind time-critical interventions and the role of multidisciplinary care. Illustrate with an example.
markScheme: Defines open fracture: communication between fracture and external environment
Primary survey priorities first (<C>ABCDE); fracture management is secondary to life threats
Gustilo–Anderson classification (I, II, IIIA–C) and its limitations (often finalised at debridement)
Early IV antibiotics within 1 hour (BOAST): strongest modifiable factor for infection
Wound care: photograph, remove gross contamination, saline-soaked dressing, avoid repeated inspection
Splintage, neurovascular assessment, tetanus status
Debridement timing: immediate for heavily contaminated/vascular injury, 12 h high energy, 24 h others
Joint orthoplastic care in specialist centre; definitive fixation and soft-tissue cover ideally within 72 h
Complications: infection, non-union, compartment syndrome, amputation; rehabilitation
Worked example with application of principles
questions.modelAnswer:
An open fracture is one in which the fracture communicates with the external environment through a breach in the skin. It carries a high risk of deep infection, non-union and, in severe cases, limb loss, so management is time-critical and multidisciplinary.

Life comes before limb. Patients with open fractures often have major trauma, so the <C>ABCDE primary survey and control of catastrophic haemorrhage take priority. Once life threats are managed, the limb is assessed for neurovascular status, wound size and contamination.

The Gustilo–Anderson classification grades open fractures from type I (small, clean wound) to type III, which is divided into IIIA (adequate soft-tissue cover), IIIB (periosteal stripping needing flap cover) and IIIC (arterial injury needing repair). Its limitations are poor inter-observer reliability and the fact that the true grade is often only clear at debridement.

The BOAST open fracture standard sets out key interventions. IV antibiotics should be given as soon as possible, ideally within an hour of injury, as early antibiotics are one of the most important modifiable factors in reducing infection. The wound is photographed so that it does not need repeated exposure, gross contamination is removed, and a saline-soaked dressing is applied. The limb is splinted and reassessed, and tetanus status addressed. Surgical debridement should occur immediately for highly contaminated wounds (agricultural, marine or sewage) or with vascular compromise, within 12 hours for other high-energy injuries and within 24 hours for others.

Severe open fractures, especially of the tibia, should be managed in a major trauma centre by a joint orthoplastic team, with definitive fixation and soft-tissue cover planned together, ideally within 72 hours. Complications include infection, compartment syndrome, non-union and, for unsalvageable limbs, amputation; rehabilitation and psychological support are essential.

For example, a motorcyclist with a tibial shaft fracture and a 12 cm contaminated wound with exposed bone (likely IIIB) is resuscitated, given IV antibiotics within an hour, has the wound photographed and dressed and the limb splinted, and is transferred to a major trauma centre for joint orthoplastic debridement, stabilisation and planned flap cover.

questions.q: Mr Ward, 63, BMI 41, with obstructive sleep apnoea and a previous note of difficult intubation, needs an emergency laparotomy for perforated diverticulitis. HR 120, BP 92/58, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. CT shows free gas and faecal contamination. He uses CPAP at night, takes metformin and ramipril, and has limited mouth opening and a thick neck. Discuss his anaesthetic assessment and plan, including airway strategy, induction, intraoperative care and postoperative destination.
markScheme: Preoperative assessment: airway (Mallampati, neck, mouth opening), previous difficult intubation records, OSA, cardiorespiratory reserve
Risk scoring (e.g. NELA risk); high-risk patient needing consultant anaesthetist and surgeon present
Resuscitation in parallel; antibiotics given; sepsis management without delaying source control
Aspiration risk: RSI indicated; NG decompression
Airway plan A–D per Difficult Airway Society; prepare videolaryngoscope, bougie, supraglottic device, front-of-neck access kit
Ramped positioning, preoxygenation (consider high-flow nasal oxygen) due to obesity and short safe apnoea time
Induction agent chosen for haemodynamic stability (e.g. ketamine or reduced propofol), vasopressors ready
Arterial line, goal-directed fluids, vasopressors, temperature, glucose monitoring
Confirm tube with waveform capnography; lung-protective ventilation
Postoperative critical care (HDU/ICU) with CPAP for OSA, opioid-sparing analgesia, VTE prophylaxis
questions.modelAnswer:
Mr Ward is a high-risk patient: he has septic shock from faecal or purulent peritonitis, morbid obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea and a documented difficult intubation. His predicted mortality on a tool such as the NELA risk calculator will be high, so the national standard is that a consultant surgeon and consultant anaesthetist are present and that postoperative critical care is booked.

Assessment should be focused and fast, as source control cannot wait. The anaesthetist reviews previous anaesthetic records for the exact airway difficulty, examines mouth opening, Mallampati class, neck movement, thyromental distance and neck circumference, and assesses cardiorespiratory reserve. Resuscitation runs in parallel: IV antibiotics should already be running, fluid boluses are given while assessing response, and early vasopressors are used rather than excessive fluid.

Two risks dominate the airway. He has a high aspiration risk from peritonitis and ileus, so a rapid sequence induction is indicated with NG decompression first. His obesity shortens the time before desaturation, and his history predicts difficult laryngoscopy. The airway plan should follow Difficult Airway Society principles: plan A with a videolaryngoscope and bougie by the most experienced operator; plan B a second-generation supraglottic airway for oxygenation; plan C face-mask ventilation; and plan D front-of-neck access, with the kit open and the team briefed. He should be ramped so the ear is level with the sternal notch and preoxygenated thoroughly, with high-flow nasal oxygen considered for apnoeic oxygenation.

Because of septic shock, the induction agent and amount are chosen for haemodynamic stability (for example ketamine or a reduced amount of propofol), with vasopressors drawn up and an arterial line ideally inserted before induction. Tube placement is confirmed with waveform capnography. Intraoperative care includes lung-protective ventilation, goal-directed fluids and vasopressors, temperature and glucose control, and serial lactate.

Afterwards, he should go to critical care for ongoing vasopressor support and possibly a period of ventilation. When extubated, he will need CPAP for his OSA, opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, VTE prophylaxis adjusted for weight and early physiotherapy.
